content.title: About
content.content: Swiss cheese with reduced sodium (535 mg sodium per 100 g) is a semi‑hard cheese known for its large holes, mild nutty flavor, and a softer finish compared to regular Swiss cheese. The lower salt content makes it suitable for those monitoring sodium intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Swiss cheese is also called “Emmental,” named after the Swiss town of Emmental.
The characteristic holes are formed by carbon dioxide released by Propionibacterium freudenreichii during aging.
Reduced sodium is achieved by replacing part of the salt with potassium salts or using specific processing techniques without altering texture.
Traditional aging ranges from 4 to 12 months; longer aging deepens the flavor.
Swiss cheese is a classic ingredient in fondue, sandwiches, and baked dishes.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Complete protein aids tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides B12, riboflavin, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic bacteria
items.content: Beneficial bacteria formed during fermentation may support gut microbiota.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: 535 mg per 100 g allows inclusion in low‑salt diets without sacrificing taste.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose; individuals with intolerance should limit consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein can occur in sensitive people.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Moderation is advised for those with cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Approximately 380 kcal per 100 g; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice thin for sandwiches, add to salads, melt in fondue, incorporate into casseroles, omelets, or enjoy as a snack. Allow the cheese to reach room temperature for a milder taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cheese in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, wrap it in wax paper to prevent drying. It stays fresh for 4‑6 weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated cappuccino is a beverage made from espresso brewed with decaf coffee beans, combined with hot milk and milk foam. It retains the characteristic flavor notes of a traditional cappuccino while lacking the stimulating effect of caffeine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by water‑process or CO₂ extraction, preserving most aromatic compounds.
Cappuccino without caffeine is often chosen by people sensitive to caffeine but who still want the coffee experience.
Traditional Italian cappuccino consists of equal parts espresso, hot milk, and milk foam.
The foam creates microscopic bubbles that trap aromatic oils, enhancing flavor.
In some countries, decaf coffee drinks are sold only in specialty cafés.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Decaf beans retain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Coffee stimulates gastric secretions, which can aid digestion even without caffeine.

items.title: Low caffeine content
items.content: Suitable for individuals with caffeine sensitivity, pregnant or nursing women.

items.title: Source of magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing aroma
items.content: The coffee aroma can have a calming effect and improve overall well‑being.

items.title: Residual caffeine
items.content: Even after decaffeination, a small amount of caffeine may remain.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: The milk foam makes the drink unsuitable for those with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Additives and flavorings
items.content: Some decaf blends may contain artificial flavorings that not everyone tolerates.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve decaf cappuccino hot, immediately after preparation to preserve the creamy foam. Optionally sprinkle cinnamon, cocoa powder, or a small amount of sugar to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep decaffeinated coffee beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Milk should be stored in the refrigerator and used within 2–3 days.

corn-ns-as-to-form-cooked.title: Corn, NS as to form, cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Corn (Zea mays) is an annual cereal plant cultivated worldwide. Cooked corn on the cob has a sweet flavor, juicy texture, and bright yellow color. It is commonly served as a side dish or used in salads, soups, and Asian-inspired recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn is one of the most important food crops, grown in over 100 countries.
There are more than 300 varieties of corn, differing in size, color, and taste.
Sweet corn, which is usually boiled, contains more sugar than field corn varieties.
Corn was domesticated in Mexico more than 7,000 years ago.
Corn kernels are used to produce starch, oil, and bio‑fuel.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant, supports the immune system, and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Provides magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals help regulate muscle and nerve function and maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Cooked corn provides about 90 kcal per 100 g, making it a good option for weight management.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn, ranging from skin rashes to respiratory issues.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Corn has a relatively high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking or sprouting lowers its level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil corn on the cob in salted water for 5‑7 minutes until tender. It can be eaten plain, added to salads, soups, chili, or used as a filling for tacos and burritos. Grilling the cob adds a smoky flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh ears in the refrigerator in a plastic bag for 3‑5 days. Frozen ears retain quality for up to 8 months when stored in an airtight container.

green-beans-frozen-cooked-with-oil.title: Green beans, frozen, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans are flash‑frozen shortly after harvest and pre‑cooked in vegetable oil. The process locks in a crisp texture, bright green color, and a mildly sweet flavor. The product is convenient for freezer storage and can be used as a quick side dish or ingredient in various recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Freezing occurs immediately after picking, preserving most of the vitamins and minerals.
Cooking in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and K.
Green beans belong to the legume family and are a good source of plant protein.
In the United States and Canada, frozen green beans are a staple in ready‑to‑heat meals.
Beans can be cultivated in open fields as well as in greenhouse systems.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin help protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup delivers about 70 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium contribute to normal blood pressure.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The product may be seasoned with salt; people with hypertension should check the sodium level.

items.title: Texture changes over time
items.content: Extended freezer storage can make the beans softer than fresh ones.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat in the microwave or a skillet, season to taste. Works well as a side for meat or fish, in salads, soups, and casseroles. Add to vegetable mixes for a quick meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, use within 6‑12 months. Do not thaw and refreeze the product.

ham-or-pork-and-potatoes-with-cheese-sau.title: Ham or pork with potatoes and cheese sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of diced ham or pork, boiled potatoes and a creamy cheese sauce. It is popular in family meals and school cafeterias, combining protein, carbohydrates and dairy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese sauce is often made from processed cheese, milk and butter.
Ham can be smoked or boiled, which changes the flavor profile.
Potatoes are usually boiled, but can be lightly fried for a crispy crust.
The dish is often baked until a golden cheese crust forms.
In some regions fresh chives or dill are added for brightness.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Ham or pork provides high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑dense carbs
items.content: Potatoes supply complex carbohydrates that give lasting satiety.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cheese sauce contributes calcium for bone health and vitamin D to aid its absorption.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat is rich in B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Keeping the potato skins adds fiber, which benefits digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham often contains a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese sauce and meat can be high in saturated fats, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with these conditions should use alternative sauces.

items.title: Proper meat cooking
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure it is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, optionally topped with fresh herbs, sour cream or tomato sauce. It pairs well with a green salad or sauerkraut.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. When frozen, it can be stored up to 1 month after cooling and placing in a freezer‑safe bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked noodles are a ready‑to‑eat product made from wheat or rice flour that becomes soft and springy after boiling. They are a staple in Asian cuisine, serving as the base for soups, salads, and quick‑cook dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Noodles typically cook in 2–5 minutes depending on thickness and type.
There are over 200 varieties of noodles, including egg, udon, soba and rice noodles.
Traditional Japanese udon is made from wheat flour, while soba is made from buckwheat.
In China, cold noodles are a popular summer dish, dressed with soy sauce and sesame oil.
Noodles can be fortified with vitamins and minerals during processing.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Noodles provide a quick source of energy thanks to their high complex carbohydrate content.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most cooked noodles contain little fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains iron and B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat noodles are rich in iron and vitamins B1, B2, which support metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture of cooked noodles aids digestion, especially for mild gastrointestinal issues.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Noodles can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Wheat noodles contain gluten and are unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Added salt
items.content: Some pre‑flavored noodles contain added salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil noodles in salted water for 2–5 minutes, then rinse with cold water. They can be added to soups, tossed in sauces, used in salads, or served as a quick‑cook base.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry noodles in a cool, dry place in an airtight container. Cooked noodles should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 2–3 days in a sealed container.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach and cheese casserole is a baked dish made of layers of fresh spinach, creamy cheese, eggs, and dairy, cooked until a golden crust forms. It combines the mild flavor of spinach with the rich aroma of melted cheese, creating a hearty and nutritious side or main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is rich in iron, vitamins A, C, K, and folate, supporting blood health and vision.
Cheeses commonly used include cheddar, mozzarella, or cottage cheese, adding flavor depth and texture.
Traditionally baked in a ceramic or glass dish for even heat distribution.
Popular in American and European cuisines as a quick way to use leftover spinach.
The recipe is easily adaptable for dietary needs, such as using plant‑based dairy alternatives.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Spinach provides non‑heme iron, which helps maintain normal blood formation and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and cheese supply B12 and B2, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: Protein
items.content: The combination of eggs, cheese, and spinach makes a complete protein source.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Spinach adds fiber, aiding digestive health.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Many cheeses are salty; choose low‑sodium or reduced‑fat options if monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Oxalates in spinach
items.content: Spinach is high in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich due to cheese and eggs; portion control is advised for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the casserole hot as a main dish, cut into portions and pair with a fresh salad or vegetable side. Cold leftovers work well in sandwiches or as a quick snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the casserole to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave or oven at 180 °C until thoroughly heated.
